01 / The beginning

Start with the part that feels confusing.

Study Bench grew from a learner’s experience of meeting anatomy as a new language. Directional terms sounded simple in isolation, yet using them confidently required a reliable reference point, a comparison, and repeated practice.

That experience became the blueprint: narrow the topic, make the relationship visible, leave room to answer, and explain the reasoning afterward. The goal is not to rush through more material. It is to build a foundation sturdy enough for what comes next.

02 / What guides us

Clarity before complexity.

Every resource should help a learner know
what to notice, practise, and revisit.

01

Make it concrete.

Definitions become useful when they are connected to a visual reference and a specific comparison.

02

Practise with purpose.

Questions should reinforce one idea at a time, then gradually ask the learner to apply it independently.

03

Explain the answer.

A correct answer matters. Understanding why it is correct makes the next question easier to reason through.

03 / The rhythm

See it. Say it.
Use it. Check it.

  1. See

    Begin with a clean reference that makes the relationship visible.

  2. Say

    Put the comparison into words instead of relying on recognition alone.

  3. Use

    Answer without the prompt and leave a trace of your reasoning on paper.

  4. Check

    Read the explanation, correct the thinking, and try the comparison again.

04 / Why answer first?

Practice should do more than measure memory.

There is a reason Study Bench asks you to try before revealing the explanation.

LEARNING SCIENCE NOTE / 001THE TESTING EFFECT

Trying to bring an answer to mind can strengthen what you remember later—not merely reveal what you already know.

Researchers call the act retrieval practice. The improvement it can produce in delayed retention is often called the testing effect. In foundational studies, learners who practised retrieving material remembered more after a delay than learners who only restudied it.

1 Retrieve→2 Check→3 Correct→4 Try again

That is the pattern behind our worksheets: answer without the prompt, check the explained key, correct the reasoning, and revisit the comparison. It is a learning method—not a guarantee—and it works best as part of thoughtful, repeated study.

Foundational study · 2006Roediger & Karpicke, “Test-enhanced learning” ↗ Follow-up study · 2008Karpicke & Roediger, “The critical importance of retrieval for learning” ↗
